signalman.text: George Stephenson built this line across the moss in 1830. Floated it on heather, brushwood and tonnes of spoil.
It sinks a little every year and they top it up. Like my pension, but with trains.

peat_cutter.text: My granddad cut peat here for the gardens. Takes eight thousand years to make. We dug it in a week.
Britain's peat bogs store more carbon than all its forests. Don't take the mickey out of the damp.

else.text: Your phone buzzes. Professor Garside, calling from what sounds like a cupboard.
{player}, I hear bog. Marvellous. Stand still and sniff. Smells a bit like pickles, yes?
That's eight thousand years of Sphagnum, holding on to carbon so the sky doesn't have to. The Enclosure, I'm told, wants to drain it for 'parking'.
Parking. On a bog. Do give the Wardens a stern look, and a battle if they insist.

botanist.text: That's sphagnum moss. It can hold twenty times its own weight in water. In the First World War they used it as wound dressing.
Chat Moss is one of the largest lowland raised bogs in England. Ten square miles of squelch.

salad_farmer.text: They drained the edges of Chat Moss for farming. Best salad leaves in the north-west. Lettuces love a black soil.
Mind the ditches. I lost a tractor in one in 1998. She's still down there, biding her time.

hermit.text: Ah. You found the brambles. Not many do.

then.text: I gave you what I had, mind. Come back for the soup when the moss is dry.

else.text: I make my own snares out of bog oak and spite. Take some. They're sturdy.
